1.station: From the summit, facing back down the climbing route, a short step down and to the left lands in the small notch on the southeast edge. The tree growing in that notch is the standard top anchor and normally already carries slings and rings. The rappel drops back onto the ledge where pitch 3 finishes.
hazards: This is the pull that hangs up most often on the descent; at least one party has had to prusik back up the stuck strand to free it
Wide clefts in the rock flanking the line will swallow a thrown rope end - feed the rope down rather than tossing it
1.pull: Check the pull direction before the last person leaves the anchor, and keep the strands out of the clefts beside the line.

2.station: The anchor on the ledge at the top of pitch 3, right where the first rappel deposits you. The ground below is scrambly, but exposed enough that most parties rappel it rather than downclimb.
hazards: A 60 m rope doubled (a 30 m rappel) finishes just short of the next tree, so the last few metres are an unroped down-scramble - expect it rather than discovering it at the rope ends. The scramble itself is short and surrounded by trees

3.station: The large, straight tree on the skier's-left side of the ledge where pitch 2 ends - the long-standing rappel tree on this descent. Since August 2024 a rock-based anchor has been added alongside it, because the tree is ageing under heavy traffic.
hazards: The tree is an ageing anchor carrying most of the traffic on the peak; use the rock backup beside it where it is in place
3.pull: The tree sits back about two metres from the lip, so the rope saws across the flat top of the ledge and this pull can be very stiff. Pull from immediately at the slung rock horn atop pitch 1 - moving any further from the ledge before pulling is what makes it stick.

4.station: Slung blocks at the top of pitch 1 - a balanced tabletop rock resting on a slung horn - which is also where you pull the previous rope from. The rappel returns you to the spot where you first roped up.
hazards: The anchor is a balanced block on a horn rather than fixed hardware; load it in line with the pull and do not shock-load or shift it

set.rappel_count_note: Four rappels on a single 60 m rope, each under 30 m, reversing the four pitches of the South Face - this is the standard descent that Northeast Slabs parties join at the summit. Two 60 m ropes let you link them into fewer, longer raps. A separate two-rappel option exists in the east gully off Pineapple Pass on two bolted chain stations (60 m rope); its second station is not directly below the first, so you rappel out east and may have to scramble a few feet up a rib to reach it - that is a different line, not part of the four-rappel tree sequence above. Some winter parties instead take two long 60 m rappels from a tree below the summit straight down to the notch.

1.station: Reached by downclimbing and simul-climbing the exposed upper West Ridge crest west from the true summit. The first bolted station is the obvious one just west of the summit - it is the one anchor on this descent nobody reports having trouble finding.
hazards: The traverse to reach it is the ultra-exposed ridge crest, with loose rock and gravel over the ledges

2.station: The station parties lose. It is not in the fall line below the first - look out to skier's left before committing to a rappel direction. Several old tat-marked stations are scattered through this gully and compete for attention; the correct continuation is the bolted pair, since the whole line was rebolted with chain anchors in 2010.
hazards: Multiple abandoned tat anchors in the same gully make it easy to commit to the wrong descent line
Rappelling straight down from station 1 takes you past the correct station

3.station: Below the upper rappels the ridge flattens out. The continuation is down the crest and then onto third-class ledges on the SOUTH side of the ridge; the next bolted station sits above the large dihedral that dominates this part of the west side.
hazards: Two southwest-facing gullies below the flat section look like the way down and are not - parties are regularly drawn into them. Bypass both and stay with the crest and the south-side ledges

4.station: The last bolted station takes you down the dihedral itself and onto the upper scree slopes.
hazards: Off the ropes it is easy to drift too far skier's left and cliff out. Traverse right, pick up the cairn across the large scree bowl, then zig-zag down to the boulder field and the approach trail

set.rappel_count_note: This is the standard, faster West Ridge descent on a single 60 m rope, and sources give either four or five rappels for it. A 2024 South Buttress party counted four: two off the summit area down the gully, then one above the big dihedral and one down it. The West Ridge route description counts five: two down to the flat part of the ridge, then three more off bolted anchors from the third-class ledges on the south side. The difference is how much of the crest between them a party downclimbs, not a disagreement about the anchors - all of them are bolted chain stations (ASCA rebolted 2010). Reversing the South Buttress directly instead takes 12 or more single-rope rappels on mixed bolt, tat and tree anchors and takes considerably longer.

1.station: Off the summit rock band the descent starts down the west/southwest side on the standard summer bolted stations - not back down the couloir you climbed.
hazards: Descending the east-side couloir instead is the documented trap: it holds no fixed anchors, so parties improvise stations on steep broken rock and old rusted pitons. The May 2025 fatal accident on this route happened that way

2.station: Second bolted station on the standard line. Short downclimbs link the stations, so expect to move between anchors on foot rather than rappelling continuously.
hazards: Loose rock on the ledges between stations, with the party below you directly in the fall line

3.station: The third rappel is the one that lands you in the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire. That notch is the aiming point for the whole upper sequence - if you are not heading toward it you are on the wrong line.
hazards: Route-finding, not steepness, is the difficulty here: several rappel lines exist on this face and only this one leads to the chockstone exit

4.station: From the notch, the final rappel takes you past the large chockstone in the West Couloir. The anchor is NOT on the chockstone itself - it is a fixed piton-and-nut station in the skier's-right wall, and a single rope gets you down past the blockage.
hazards: Largely free-hanging as you clear the chockstone, with no wall contact to steady you or to fend off a spin
The exit below traverses under South Early Winters Spire's southwest rib into Spire Gully, which postholes badly in soft snow
4.pull: Pull clear of the chockstone's underside - the strands hang free past it and a knot pulled up against the block is awkward to reach from below.

set.rappel_count_note: Four rappels plus downclimbing, on a single 60 m rope, using the standard summer bolted stations down the west side to the North/South Early Winters Spire notch, then the piton-and-nut anchor in the skier's-right wall to get past the West Couloir chockstone. The competing figure of about six belongs to a DIFFERENT line: a newer, fully bolted rappel route down the right side of the West Face, roughly six stations spaced about 100 ft (30 m) apart. That line does not include the chockstone rappel; a 60 m rope only just works on it, and on its third station you have to reach down to clip in before letting the rope run through, so knot the ends. Do not mix stations between the two lines.

1.station: From the summit keep going east through a notch, then down the northeast face and its snowfield to a notch on the East Ridge. The first station is at that notch, and the rappel drops east off the ridge. A single 60 m rope reaches.
hazards: Getting to the station means a steep snow traverse on the northeast face - carry axe and crampons even on a rock route in summer

2.station: Do not rappel the fall line from station 1. Traverse skier's left (north) and down a short, loose gully. A rappel is possible here and many parties simply downclimb it - which is why counts of three and four both appear for this descent.
hazards: The gully is short but loose, and the rope and the party above sit directly over whoever is below

A rap anchor on a tree is visible on this part of the descent and leads onto improbably steep ground where a single rope can leave you hanging in space. The usable stations are further skier's left, closer to the northeast ridge - reposition rather than committing to the tree

3.station: Below the gully, cut back through a notch onto the East Face. The last two stations are on that face, and this is the first of them.
hazards: Missing the notch and continuing down the north side puts you above unrappelled terrain with no stations

4.station: The final station drops to the slopes near the Argonaut-Colchuck col, where the technical descent ends and the walk to Colchuck Lake begins.
hazards: Allow the time: parties report roughly four hours from summit to the base even with the stations found first try

set.rappel_count_note: Four single-rope rappels (60 m) from the East Ridge notch down to the Argonaut-Colchuck col, and this is a traverse descent off the east side - not a reversal of the arete. Both the Mountaineers route page and Mountain Project describe the same sequence, and a 2022 party counted 'the 1st of 4 rappels'. Three is also correct for a party that downclimbs the short loose gully at station 2 instead of rappelling it; the difference is that one optional rappel, not a rope-configuration difference.

1.station: At the east end of the summit ridge, after the long loose traverse along ledges below the crest. The first rappel is a full rope-stretcher on a single 60 m down to a big block; parties who want shorter, more controllable pitches split it into two.
hazards: The alternative to the whole rappel sequence is downclimbing the loose gully immediately to climber's right of the rap line - parties on the two lines put rock down on each other, so agree on one or the other before splitting up

2.station: The big block itself - the landing for the rope-stretcher, or the intermediate station if you split it. Most of the anchors from here down are slings wrapped around large blocks.
hazards: Several of the wrapped blocks on this ridge are genuinely suspect. Push and check each one is seated before you weight the sling, rather than trusting that it held for the last party

3.station: First of two or three further rappels working down the crest below the big block.
hazards: Old cord and webbing of very mixed age; carry plenty of spare cord and rebuild the worst stations rather than adding to them

4.station: Continues down the crest; a 60 m single rope covers every station on this section.
hazards: Sustained loose rock - this ridge is a serious descent in its own right, not a walk-off, and most parties take three to five hours on it

5.station: The last of the crest rappels, ending where the ground turns to heather.
hazards: Wet heather over rock is slick and hides the edges of steps

6.station: After the heather you downclimb rather than rappel, and the next station is slightly hidden - it is easy to walk past it and end up downclimbing ground you should have rappelled. Find it before you commit to descending further.
hazards: A hidden station means the common error here is going too far and having to reclimb loose ground to reach it

7.station: From that hidden station, the last rappels drop to the Cascade-Johannesburg col, where the route joins Doug's Direct back toward Cascade Pass.
hazards: The col and the terrain below it are exposed to anything the ridge sheds - do not regroup directly beneath the rappel line

set.rappel_count_note: Up to seven rappels on a single 60 m rope down the East Ridge to the Cascade-Johannesburg col: one rope-stretcher (or two shorter) to a big block, two or three more to the heather, then a downclimb to a slightly hidden station and two more to the col. Six to eight are all reported and the spread is a choice, not a conflict - the first rappel can be split, the gully to climber's right can be downclimbed instead, and how much heather you rappel versus scramble varies. Bring cord: many stations are slings around blocks and are routinely rebuilt.

1.station: From the summit, walk east and drop onto the north face. Getting onto the first station is awkward - you squeeze into a small chute to reach it - and this is the shortest rappel of the sequence. An old bolted station is occasionally reported as an alternative right at the top.
hazards: The chute above the anchor is a rope-catcher; at least one party jammed the rope on this first pull and needed a progress-capture pulley to free it
1.pull: Set the knot clear of the constriction and pull from directly below the station, not off to one side - the chute is what traps the strand.

2.station: Below the first drop, every station is a slung natural anchor - blocks and chockstones carrying webbing and tat, with little or no fixed gear. They are not stacked in a single fall line, so stop at the rope ends and look around before assuming you have overshot one.
hazards: Locating the stations, not the rappelling, is the crux of this descent; parties describe the raps themselves as easy but the sequence confusing

3.station: Continues down the north-face line on the same style of slung natural station.
hazards: The tat is whatever previous parties left and varies widely in age - carry cord and replace anything sun-bleached rather than backing it up and moving on

4.station: The last rappel puts you onto a good ledge system. From there traverse west and scramble down to the base of the route - do not go looking for further anchors below the ledge.
hazards: Parties who keep rappelling past the ledge end up off the established line on ground with no stations

set.rappel_count_note: The station count here is a rope-configuration question and all the published figures are right about different setups. On two ropes a party got down in three (two double-length rappels and one single). On a single 60 m rope doubled - a 30 m rappel - parties report four or five, one noting a shorter first rappel followed by four that were 30 m rope-stretchers, and that they 'probably could have done 4 and scrambled the 5th'. The four stations listed here are the single-rope sequence; if you are on 30 m rappels rather than 25 m, expect to reach the ledge in four or five, and treat the shorter first drop as normal.

1.station: From the West Ridge notch - reached by downclimbing and short rappels along the ridge from the summit - the descent takes the rock rib bordering the snow couloir rather than the couloir's own fall line. The first station is on that rib. One rope works for these rappels.
hazards: Everything in this gully system funnels rockfall, and party-induced rockfall from groups above is the main objective danger of the descent. The rib line exists to keep you out of the channel - do not shortcut into the gully to save a rappel

2.station: Successive stations continue down the rib. Anchors are plentiful here because this is the standard way off anything on Forbidden, so the problem is choosing among them rather than finding one.
hazards: Abundant anchors of very mixed vintage; some are old slings with no hardware

3.station: Mid-sequence on the rib. Downclimbing and simul-downclimbing between stations is normal and is how parties get the count down.
hazards: Carry spare webbing and rap rings - stations on this line routinely need backing up or rebuilding before use

4.station: Lower rib, approaching the base of the gully system.
hazards: The rock gully alongside can be wet and loose; a wet rope pulled across it picks up grit and jams

5.station: Before rappelling the last cliff band onto snow, look for the station off to the LEFT rather than continuing straight down. Parties have found the lowest slung-boulder anchor stripped by a descending group, so be prepared to build one.
hazards: The landing is at the moat/bergschrund between rock and snow, and crossing it can be the hardest move of the descent
The lowest anchor has been removed by other parties before now - carry enough gear and cord to leave a station behind
Dry late-season conditions add rappels here rather than removing them

set.rappel_count_note: About five single-rope rappels, roughly 400 ft total, down the rock rib beside the snow couloir - Mountain Project gives 'five or six single rope rappels from here back to the snowfield' for the same line. Three is reported in good early-season snow, when much of the couloir is downclimbed instead, and six to seven in dry late-season conditions when the snow has pulled back off the rock. All of these are single-rope figures; two ropes roughly halves them. Do not reverse the Northeast Face itself.

1.station: The traverse finishes by descending Forbidden, so this is Forbidden's own descent. From the summit ridge, the first rappels are off in-situ slings on horns and blocks along the West Ridge crest, with simul-downclimbing between them, heading for the West Ridge notch where most parties left a cache.
hazards: The crest anchors are slings over natural features, not fixed hardware - inspect and back up rather than clipping and going

2.station: The second station of the descent is the one that is offset: it sits at climber's LEFT. Every other station on the sequence is either straight below the last one or at climber's right, so if you are hunting left further down you are looking in the wrong place.
hazards: Rappelling the fall line here takes you past the station

3.station: Last of the ridge-crest rappels, landing at the West Ridge notch. From here the descent switches to the gully system back toward Boston Basin.
hazards: This is where parties regroup and where rockfall from anyone still on the ridge above concentrates

4.station: First station below the notch. The rappel line follows the fixed anchors on the small arete bordering the gully rather than the gully's own fall line, which is what keeps you out of the rockfall channel.
hazards: All of the gullies here are full of loose rock and party-induced rockfall is the single biggest danger on this descent

5.station: Continues down the arete beside the gully. Stations are numerous - this is the standard way off Forbidden and off the traverse - so expect several options and pick the one that keeps you out of the channel.
hazards: Anchors of mixed age and quality; carry webbing and rings to rebuild

6.station: Mid-gully. Stations are visible from roughly a rope length away once you know to look at the arete rather than the gully bed.
hazards: Wet, loose rock in the gully bed grits up a rope and makes pulls stiff

7.station: Continues down; downclimbing between stations is normal and is how the count varies between parties.
hazards: Rope ends thrown into the gully bed snag on loose blocks

8.station: Lower gully, approaching the last cliff band above the snow.
hazards: Anchor quality does not improve toward the bottom - the lowest slung-boulder anchor has been found stripped by a previous descending party

9.station: Second-to-last station. Before you commit to rappelling the last cliff onto the snow, look for the station off to the LEFT rather than going straight over the edge.
hazards: Going over the last cliff on the wrong line leaves you above the moat with no anchor within reach

10.station: The final rappel down the last cliff band onto the snowfield at the base of the cat scratch gully.
hazards: The landing crosses the moat between rock and snow and this can be genuinely difficult - the first person down should carry a picket, ice axe and crampons so they can climb out of the moat if needed
Rope up again immediately below: the ground below is glacier remnant, and the waterfall slabs further down toward Boston Basin have killed people (that hazard is on the walk out, not on this rappel)
10.pull: Pull before anyone commits to the moat crossing - a stuck rope with the party split across a moat is the worst place on the descent to be.

set.rappel_count_note: Ten rappels in all on a single rope brings you from Forbidden's summit back to the base of the cat scratch gully - roughly three down the West Ridge crest to the notch, then the rest down the gully system. That total is the traverse's own route description and matches independent trip reports (one party logged 'several' to regain the notch and then six more to the glacier remnants). Two ropes roughly halves it; Mountain Project gives 'five or six single rope rappels' for the rock rib below the notch alone. Per-rappel lengths are not published anywhere for this descent - the stored figures are estimates, not measurements.
